1     Set theory
In this section we review/develop the set-theoretic background for the course.

1.1     Basic definitions
Naive definition: A set is an aggregate of things, called elements of the set. We
usually use capital letters to denote sets, such as A, B, C, and lowercase letters
for elements, such as a, b, c. The notation a ∈ A means that a is an element of
the set A. We write a ∈ / A to mean that a is not an element of the set A.
Example 1.1. Some basic examples of sets include:
    • The natural numbers N = {1, 2, 3, . . .}

    • The integers Z = {. . . , −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, . . .}
    • The real numbers R

Set calculus A set A is a subset of a set B if every element of A is also an
element of B. We write A ⊆ B to denote that A is a subset of B. If A is a
subset of B but not equal to B, we say that A is a proper subset of B and denote
it by A ⊊ B.
    We let P(A) denote the power set of A, which is the set of all subsets of A.
    We say two sets A and B are equal if they have the same elements, that is,
if A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A. We write A = B to denote that A and B are equal.
    We let A\B denote the set difference of A and B, which is the set of elements
in A that are not in B. Formally, A\B = {x ∈ A : x ∈    / B}. When B ⊆ A, we
say A\B is the complement of B in A.
    The empty set, denoted ∅, is a set that contains no elements. It is a subset
of every set.

1.2    Functions
Cartesian product The Cartesian product of two sets A and B, denoted
A × B, is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) where a ∈ A and b ∈ B:

                        A × B = {(a, b) : a ∈ A, b ∈ B}.

   Formally, an ordered pair can be defined as follows and define the cartesian
product as a set of sets:
                            (a, b) := {{a}, {a, b}}.
Remark 1.5. If one set is empty, then the Cartesian product is also empty:

                               A × ∅ = ∅ × B = ∅.

Definition 1.6. A function f : A → B is a subset of the Cartesian product
A × B such that for any a ∈ A, there exists a unique b ∈ B such that (a, b) ∈ f .

1.3     Relations
Definition 1.10. A relation on a set S is any subset R ⊆ S × S. If (a, b) ∈ R,
we say that a is related to b and write aRb.
   A relation R is called
   • reflexive if aRa for all a ∈ S;
   • symmetric if aRb implies bRa;
   • transitive if aRb and bRc imply aRc;
   • antisymmetric if aRb and bRa imply a = b.

1.3.1   Equivalence relations
Definition 1.11. We say that R is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive,
symmetric, and transitive. An equivalence relation is usually denoted by ∼ and
if (a, b) ∈∼ we write a ∼ b.
Example 1.12. The relation R on Z defined by aRb if and only if a − b is even
is an equivalence relation.

Example 1.13. Let f : A → B be any function. The relation R on A defined
by aRb if and only if f (a) = f (b) is an equivalence relation.
Example 1.14. Let T denote the set of all triangles in the plane. The relation
R on T defined by △1 R△2 if and only if △1 is similar to △2 is an equivalence
relation.
Definition 1.15. Let A be a non empty set. For any a ∈ A, we define the
equivalence class of a as
                                    [a] = { b ∈ A : a ∼ b }.
Example 1.16. Consider the equivalence relation ∼ on Z defined by a ∼ b if
and only if a − b is even. Then, there are two equivalence classes: the even
integers and the odd integers. Specifically,
    [0] = {. . . − 4, −2, 0, 2, 4, 6, . . . },         [1] = {. . . − 5, −3, −1, 1, 3, 5, . . . }.

nonempty subsets {Ai }i∈I such that:

Example 1.18. Consider the set A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. Then, {{1, 2}, {3}, {4, 5}}
is a partition of A.
Example 1.19. For any set A, we call {{a}}a∈A the discrete partition of A
and we call {A} the trivial partition of A.
    We denote by Part(A) the set of all partitions of A and by EqRel(A) the set
of all equivalence relations on A.

There is a one-to-one correspondence between partitions of A and equivalence

1.3.2   Partial orders
Definition 1.21. A relation R on A is a partial order if it is reflexive, antisym-
metric, and transitive. A partial order is usually denoted by ≤. A set equipped
with a partial order is called a partially ordered set or poset, and is denoted by
(A, ≤). When a ≤ b and a ̸= b, we write a < b.
Example 1.22. Consider the set of real numbers R with the usual order relation
≤. This is a partial order because it is reflexive (every number is less than or
equal to itself), antisymmetric (if a ≤ b and b ≤ a, then a = b), and transitive
(if a ≤ b and b ≤ c, then a ≤ c).

the set of all subsets of A. Define, for B, C ∈ P(A),

                             B≤C        ⇐⇒       B ⊆ C.

Then (P(A), ≤) is a partial order.

There is one case when the notion of maximal elements coincides with that
of largest elements: when the poset is totally ordered.
Definition 1.31 (Linear (total) order). A partial order ≤ on a set A is a linear
(or total) order if for all a, b ∈ A one has a ≤ b or b ≤ a (comparability).
Remark 1.32. A minimal element in a linear poset is also the smallest element.
Similarly, a maximal element is also the largest element.
Definition 1.33 (Well-order). A linear poset (A, ≤) is well-ordered if every
nonempty subset B ⊆ A has a minimal element.
Example 1.34.      • The set of natural numbers N = {0, 1, 2, . . .} with the
    usual order ≤ is well-ordered. Be careful here and ask yourself why. This
    can be either taken as an axiom in Peano Axioms or proved under ZF.
   • The set of real numbers R with the usual order ≤ is not well-ordered. [0, 1]
     is not well-ordered as well.
Example 1.35.         • We define the lexicographic order on N × N as follows:
    for (m1 , n1 ), (m2 , n2 ) ∈ N × N, we say that (m1 , n1 ) ≤ (m2 , n2 ) if either
    m1 < m2 or m1 = m2 and n1 ≤ n2 . Then, (N × N, ≤) is a well-ordered
    set.
   • We can similarly define the lexicographic order on Nk for any finite k ∈ N,
     which makes (Nk , ≤) a well-ordered set as well.
   • However, the lexicographic order on NN is not well-ordered: consider the
      subset B = {(2, 1, 1, . . .) > (1, 2, 1, . . .) > . . .}. Then, B has no minimal
      element.
   The lexicographic order on NN is not well-ordered. In fact, no one has found
an explicit well-order on NN so far. However, it turns out that in theory, one
can find a partial order on NN so that it is well-ordered.
Theorem 1.36 (Well-ordering theorem). Every set can be well-ordered.

the poset to be well-ordered, then the situation changes. We start with the

sets, Then
   1. f (0A ) = 0B ;
   2. for any a ∈ A, f ([0A , a]) = [0B , f (a)] and f ([0A , a)) = [0B , f (a)).

f (a), we have a′ ≤ a, and thus a′ ∈ [0A , a]. This gives us f ([0A , a]) = [0B , f (a)],
proving (2).

1.4    Axiom of Choice
The most commonly used axiomatic system for mathematics is the Zermelo-
Fraenkel set theory (ZF).
   • ZFC with the Axiom of Choice
   • ZF without the Axiom of Choice

   (Axiom of Choice) If {Ai }i∈I is a family of nonempty pairwise disjoint sets,
there is a set B ⊂ ∪Ai such that B ∩ Ai is exactly one element for all i ∈ I.
   What if the sets are not disjoint?

4.1     Convergence in Topological Spaces
We will try to answer the following questions:

    1. Can we define sequential convergence in general topological spaces?

    2. If so, does this convergence describe the notion of topology?

   In metric space setting, we have the notion of convergence of a sequence (in
the language of open balls):
Proposition 4.1. A sequence (xn )n∈N in a metric space X converges to a point
x ∈ X if and only if for every ϵ > 0, there exists N ∈ N such that xn ∈ Bϵ (x)
for all n ≥ N .
    This motivates the following definition in general topological spaces:

Definition 4.2. A sequence (xn )n∈N in a topological space X is said to converge
to a point x ∈ X if for every neighbourhood U of x, there exists N ∈ N such
that xn ∈ U for all n ≥ N .
Problem 4.3. A sequence (xn ) in a metric space converges in the metric sense
if and only if it converges in the topological sense defined above.

Proposition 5.24. Every sequence has a unique limit in a topological space.
Proof. When X is Hausdorff, suppose that a sequence (xn ) converges to both

V such that x ∈ U and y ∈ V . Since (xn ) → x, there exists N1 such that for all
n ≥ N1 , we have xn ∈ U . Similarly, since (xn ) → y, there exists N2 such that
for all n ≥ N2 , we have xn ∈ V . Let N = max{N1 , N2 }. Then, for all n ≥ N ,
we have xn ∈ U and xn ∈ V , contradicting the fact that U and V are disjoint.
Hence, the limit is unique.

b0 is the greatest element).
Proof. Let U be an open cover of [a, b] where a < b. Define

        S = {x ∈ [a, b] : [a, x] can be covered by a finite subcover of U}.

It is clear that a ∈ S and if x ∈ S, then [a, x] ⊂ S. Since S is clearly upper-
bounded by b, we let c = sup S, i.e., the least upper bound of S. We will show
that c ∈ S and c = b.
     Clearly c ≤ b. If (a, c) is empty, then a = c ∈ S. Suppose (a, c) is nonempty.
Then, we have that [a, c) ⊂ S. Let Uc be an open set in U containing c. By the
definition of the order topology, there exists some (d, e) such that c ∈ (d, e) ⊆ Uc .
There must be some x ∈ (d, c) otherwise sup S ≤ d < c. Then, we know x ∈ S
and hence [a, x] can be covered by a finite subcover Ux of U. Note that Ux ∪{Uc }
is a finite subcover of [a, c]. This implies that c ∈ S.
     Suppose c < b. Now we consider the interval (c, b). Let T = {x ∈ [c, b] :
[c, x] = {c}} and let y = sup T . Note that y ≤ b. If y = c, then the open set
Uc containing c also contains some element z of (c, b), and hence [x, z] can be

we must have y > c. But then the interval [a, y] can be covered by a finite
subcover of U by considering an open set around y, contradicting the definition
of c. Hence, we must have c = b.

cover. This completes the proof.

6.2    Tychonoff ’s theorem
There are multiple proofs of Tychonoff’s theorem. You can check Munkres
book for such proofs. We will give a proof using nets here which is somewhat
conceptually clean.
    We know that if a net has a cluster point, then it has a subnet that converges
to that cluster point. Then, is there any special kind of net such that if it has
a cluster point, then it converges to that cluster point? The answer is yes, and
one kind of such nets is called ultranets.
Definition 6.42. A net {xλ } in a set X is an ultranet if for any subset S ⊂ X,
the net is eventually in S or eventually in X \ S (there exists λ0 such that either
xλ ∈ S for all λ ≥ λ0 or xλ ∈ X \ S for all λ ≥ λ0 ).

Example 6.43. Any constant net is an ultranet. Any eventually constant net
is an ultranet. If Λ has a greatest element λ0 , then any net indexed by Λ is an
ultranet as it is eventually constant at xλ0 .
   One immediate consequence of this definition is the following lemma.

Lemma 6.44. An ultranet converges to each of its cluster points.
Proof. Let {xλ } be an ultranet in X and let x ∈ X be a cluster point of the net.
Given any open neighbourhood U of x, since {xλ } is an ultranet, it is eventually
in U or eventually in X \ U . Since x is a cluster point, it cannot be eventually
in X \ U . Hence, it is eventually in U . Therefore, {xλ } converges to x.

Definition 6.50. A topological space X is said to be locally compact if for
every point x ∈ X, there exists an open neighbourhood U of x and a compact
set K such that U ⊆ K.
Example 6.51. Any compact space is locally compact.

Example 6.52. R is locally compact. For each x ∈ R, we pick the open

compact and R is not compact. This is a contradiction. Therefore, there does

Proof. Let P be a path component contained in a component C. If P ̸= C,
then let Q be the union of all other path components contained in C. By the
theorem above, we know C is open. Then, by the theorem again, P and Q are
open in C and hence separate C, contradicting connectedness of C.
Corollary 7.39. A connected, locally path connected space X is path connected.

Proof. So X is a single component, which is also a single path component.
Corollary 7.40. An open connected subset of Rn is path connected.
Proof. Any open subset of Rn is locally path connected.

Totally disconnected spaces
Definition 7.41. A space X is totally disconnected iff the components of X
are singletons.

Example 7.42. The space Q of rational numbers (with the subspace topology
from R) is totally disconnected.
   Its complement R \ Q is also totally disconnected.
Example 7.43. The Cantor set is totally disconnected.
